core: Why countries trade and what trade does for them (the gains from trade)
Exports and imports as the two directions of international trade
The balance of trade: trade surplus vs trade deficit, and reading a deficit correctly
That a trade deficit is not simply 'losing' — it is financed by an offsetting inflow of financial capital
The distributional reality: trade produces aggregate gains but creates winners AND losers (e.g. displaced import-competing workers), motivating adjustment policy
Positive-vs-normative control: the aggregate gains-from-trade result is broadly settled; free-trade-vs-protection policy is contested and must be presented neutrally
supporting: Sources of gains beyond comparative advantage: greater variety, economies of scale, competition and innovation
Intra-industry trade between similar high-income economies
Splitting up the value chain across countries
Factor endowments (Heckscher-Ohlin) as one determinant of comparative advantage (named only)
outOfScope: The Ricardian numeric proof / derivation of comparative advantage (owned by economics:foundations:comparative-advantage)
The mechanics and welfare analysis of tariffs and other trade barriers (owned by economics:foundations:tariffs)
The broad social/political phenomenon of globalization (owned by economics:foundations:globalization)

claims.claim: Nearly all economists agree that trade among nations makes participating countries and the world better off overall.

Trade is driven by comparative rather than absolute advantage: a country benefits by exporting goods in which its opportunity cost is lowest and importing the rest, even when a partner is more productive at everything.

Gains from trade also come from greater product variety, economies of scale, and pro-competitive pressure that spurs innovation — not only from comparative advantage; about 60% of U.S. and European trade is intra-industry trade.
The balance of trade is the difference between a country's exports and imports of goods and services; exports exceeding imports is a surplus, imports exceeding exports is a deficit.
The U.S. ran a goods-and-services trade deficit of $773.4 billion in 2023 (exports $3,053.5 billion, imports $3,826.9 billion), down from $951.2 billion in 2022.

A trade deficit is not simply money 'lost' abroad; by the national saving and investment identity it is financed by a matching net inflow of financial capital from foreigners investing in the country.

Even when a country gains in aggregate from trade, not every individual or firm is better off: buyers of cheaper imports gain while import-competing domestic producers and their workers can lose, sometimes in absolute terms, which motivates adjustment policy.
The aggregate gains-from-trade result is settled positive economics, but whether and how to protect specific domestic industries (free trade vs protection) is a contested normative policy question.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether governments should restrict trade to protect domestic industries (free trade vs protectionism).
positions: Free-trade view: barriers reduce aggregate efficiency and living standards; the country as a whole gains from importing goods produced more cheaply abroad.
Protection view: specific industries, workers, and communities are harmed by import competition and may warrant temporary protection, industrial policy, or strong adjustment support.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented neutrally as a genuine normative policy debate. The lesson labels the aggregate gains-from-trade result as broadly settled positive economics while treating the policy response (protect or not, and how) as contested, and it points to adjustment policy without endorsing a particular stance.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Macroeconomics 3e, 20.1 Absolute and Comparative Advantage
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports the definitions of absolute advantage ('can produce more of that good') and comparative advantage ('produce a good at a lower cost in terms of other goods'), that specialization by comparative advantage lets both countries consume beyond their production possibility frontiers, and the broad agreement that trade raises living standards. The numeric Ricardian derivation belongs to the comparative-advantage topic; referenced here, not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Macroeconomics 3e, 20.3 Intra-Industry Trade between Similar Economies
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports: intra-industry trade (trade of goods within the same industry) is about 60% of U.S. and European trade; gains among similar high-income economies come from specialized learning, economies of scale (falling average cost with volume), splitting up the value chain across countries, and pro-competitive pressure that drives innovation and consumer choice/variety.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Macroeconomics 3e, 10.1 Measuring Trade Balances
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports definitions of trade balance (difference between exports and imports of goods and services), trade surplus (exports exceed imports), trade deficit (imports exceed exports), merchandise trade balance (goods only), and current account balance (goods, services, income, and transfers).

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Macroeconomics 3e, 10.4 The National Saving and Investment Identity
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports the framing that a trade deficit corresponds to a net inflow of financial capital from abroad: domestic investment can exceed domestic saving only if capital flows in from other countries, so a trade deficit is financed by foreign investment rather than being money simply 'lost.'

sourceRecords.title: International Trade: Commerce among Nations (Back to Basics)
sourceRecords.notes: Author Brad McDonald, IMF Finance & Development 'Back to Basics.' imf.org returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher; read via an Internet Archive capture of the same PDF. Supports: most economists agree trade makes the world better off; trade follows comparative not absolute advantage; buyers of cheaper imports usually gain more than domestic sellers lose, yet not every individual or firm is better off and trade can worsen the domestic income distribution (winners and losers); trade opening brings adjustment and dislocation to firms/industries that cannot compete; gains also come from greater variety and pro-competitive forces. Only short attributed facts used; prose original.
